body_ar:
عرف التجويد تعريفا قاصرا فقال:

وهو إعطاء الحروف حقها** من صفة لها ومستحقها

قال إن التجويد هو في الاصطلاح إعطاء الحروف حقها وحق الحروف هو صفاتها اللازمة صفاتها الأصلية وهي هذه الصفات الثماني عشرة فهذا حق الحروف، ومستحقها في الاصطلاح هو الصفات العارضة، الصفات العارضة التي ذكرنا بعضها ولم نحط بها، كالغنة وكالترقيق والتفخيم وغير ذلك فهذه الصفات تسمى الصفات العارضة، فهذا اصطلاح، وإلا فلا فرق في اللغة بين الحق والمستحق، لأن الحق مستحق يستحقه صاحبه، قال:

وهو إعطاء الحروف حقها** من صفة لها ومستحقها
body_en:
He defined the rules of Qur'anic recitation (tajwīd) with a definition that falls short, saying:

*And it is the giving to the letters of their due, of the quality belonging to them, and of what they merit.*

He said that tajwid, in technical usage, is the giving to the letters of their due; and the due of the letters is their necessary qualities, their original qualities, which are these eighteen qualities — this is the letters' due. And "what they merit", in technical usage, is the accidental qualities: the accidental qualities, some of which we have mentioned without covering them exhaustively, such as nasalisation, thinning, thickening and so on. These qualities are called the accidental qualities. So this is a technical usage; otherwise there is no difference in the language between "a due" and "what is merited", because a due is something merited, which the one entitled to it merits. He said:

*And it is the giving to the letters of their due, of the quality belonging to them, and of what they merit.*

flags.context: The opening clause of the record, introducing Ibn al-Jazari's definition of tajwid.
flags.note: qāṣir here is the Sheikh's own critical judgement on the author's definition — that it does not take in everything it should. It is not a neutral description, and it must not be softened into a compliment or strengthened into a charge of error. The technical sense in logic (a definition that is not co-extensive with what it defines) may be what is meant; a reviewer should confirm which.

The published page carries only the opening excerpt of this tape; the Arabic breaks off and the full text is offered on the site as a downloadable Word document. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. Nothing has been supplied to complete it.
This record begins mid-discussion, with no opening formula; the beginning of the tape is not in the source.

The line of verse is the base text of al-Jazariyyah, quoted twice by the Sheikh — once before his comment and once after it. It is rendered as prose in italics per house style, and the repetition has been kept.
The double asterisk ** in the Arabic is the source's hemistich divider, not an editorial mark.

'Their due' (ḥaqquhā) and 'what they merit' (mustaḥaqquhā) are the technical terms the whole passage turns on; they have been rendered consistently and the Arabic distinction is explained by the Sheikh himself.

al-Jazariyyah is the versified primer on Qur'anic recitation by Ibn al-Jazari, and 'the author' throughout this series is Ibn al-Jazari. The series title is left transliterated and untranslated. Articles 436-446 are tapes of this one series; their tape numbering in the titles does not run in the same order as the article IDs.
